one_liner: ANSI C write-only XLSX library; same API family as Python XlsxWriter, about 4.4x faster than it on a 200k-cell sheet.
what_it_does: Creates Excel 2007+ .xlsx files from C: numbers, strings, formulas, formats, charts, images, data validation, conditional formatting, tables, comments and macros. The API is a C transliteration of the same author's Python XlsxWriter (workbook_new, workbook_add_worksheet, worksheet_write_string/number, workbook_close), so porting code is mechanical, but it is a C library, not a Python drop-in. It cannot read or modify existing files. Output goes to a file or, with lxw_workbook_options.output_buffer, to a memory buffer.
how_it_is_fast: Mostly it is compiled C doing what the Python library does in the interpreter: cells are malloc'd structs kept in per-worksheet red-black trees (BSD tree.h) keyed by row and column, shared strings are deduplicated in a red-black tree with strcmp, and the cell-writing loop bypasses the generic XML writer and fprintf's each <c> element directly. Each XML part is written to a temp file (tmpfileplus) or, with USE_MEM_FILE, an open_memstream buffer, then deflated by bundled minizip at Z_DEFAULT_COMPRESSION. constant_memory mode flushes each row as the next one starts and writes inline strings, so memory stays at about one row. The optional USE_DTOA_LIBRARY build swaps printf('%.16G') for Milo Yip's Grisu-style emyg_dtoa, which the docs say is 40-50 percent faster on numeric data (no numbers published).
when_to_use: Generating reports or data exports as .xlsx from C or C++ services where Python XlsxWriter or openpyxl is the bottleneck or the runtime is unavailable.
Large row-ordered exports (millions of cells) with constant_memory mode, where memory must stay flat regardless of sheet size.
Workbooks that need real Excel features (formats, charts, conditional formatting, data validation, images, tables) rather than a bare CSV-to-XLSX dump.
Embedded or portable builds: ANSI C, only zlib required, builds on Linux, BSDs, macOS, iOS, Windows (MSVC, MinGW), 32/64-bit and big-endian targets.
As the engine under a higher-level binding: R's writexl and other language wrappers already sit on it.
when_not_to_use: Reading, editing or round-tripping existing .xlsx files: it is write-only; use a reader such as xlsxio or openpyxl.

When rust_xlsxwriter is an option: the same author's own hyperfine run has rust_xlsxwriter with its zlib feature at 152.6 ms versus 210.9 ms for libxlsxwriter on the same 200k-cell sheet (1.38x faster).

Multi-core throughput on one workbook: the docs say the library is single-threaded and 'optimized but not highly optimized'; each string write does a calloc, strdup and tree insert, then frees the copy if the string already exists.
Writing out of row order or editing earlier rows in constant_memory mode: data must arrive row by row, and inline strings can grow the file 20-100 percent and are unsupported by some viewers.

Programs running under a decimal-comma locale with the default build: numbers are formatted with locale-dependent fprintf, which produced corrupt files (issue #64); build with USE_DTOA_LIBRARY or force the C locale.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (Makefile builds libxlsxwriter.a and .so; CMake 3.16+ and zig build also provided)
integration.dependencies: zlib (CMake requires 1.2.8+); bundled minizip (or USE_SYSTEM_MINIZIP), tmpfileplus temp files (or USE_STANDARD_TMPFILE / USE_MEM_FILE), Openwall MD5 for image dedup (or USE_OPENSSL_MD5 / USE_NO_MD5), optional emyg_dtoa
integration.min_toolchain: ANSI C (the Makefile compiles with -ansi -pedantic -O3); README lists GCC, Clang, Xcode, MSVC 2015, ICC, TCC, MinGW and MinGW-w64
integration.platforms: Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, macOS, iOS, Windows, MSYS/MSYS2, Cygwin; 32 and 64 bit; big and little endian; no SIMD or arch-specific code
integration.thread_safety: Not documented beyond 'the library is currently single threaded'; a workbook and its worksheets must be driven from one thread. Separate workbooks share no obvious mutable globals in the code read, but this is not a documented guarantee.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the C function names and options mirror Python XlsxWriter's methods one to one, so translating code is easy, but it is a different language; Python callers need a wrapper (the Impeller Cython wrapper targets a modified fork, not upstream).

gotchas: The default build formats doubles with fprintf('%.16G'), which is locale-dependent (decimal comma under de_DE corrupts the file, issue #64; the docs suggest setlocale/uselocale or USE_DTOA_LIBRARY, which is off by default) and keeps only 16 significant digits, so doubles that need 17 digits are not written exactly.

Even in standard mode every XML part is first written to a temp file in the system tmp dir (or tmpdir option) before zipping; on hosts with /tmp in RAM, or without a writable tmp dir, use the tmpdir option or USE_MEM_FILE (not available with MSVC).
In constant_memory mode, writing in column-major order silently keeps only the first column (docs), and worksheet_set_row, merge ranges and formatting changes apply only to the current row.

Fixed memory-safety bugs on non-benchmarked paths show the attack surface: stack overflow in worksheet_set_selection (#447, 2024), read overflows in cell-name parsing in utility.c (#459, 2024), heap overflow with 256+ item data-validation lists and quadratic memory in default table columns (fixed 2026-07-07, after release 1.2.4); take a build from main or newer than 1.2.4 when inputs are untrusted.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over XLSX I/O (xlsxio) when the job is writing richly formatted workbooks with charts, validation or conditional formatting; xlsxio's catalogued evidence is for reading .xlsx, which libxlsxwriter cannot do at all. Pick it over DuckDB, Polars or the CSV parsers only when the deliverable must be a native Excel file rather than CSV or a dataframe.
verified_claims_summary: In rust_xlsxwriter's performance docs, written by the same author as libxlsxwriter and Python XlsxWriter, hyperfine (warmup 3) timed whole processes writing a 4,000 x 50 sheet of alternating 12345 and 'Foo': C/libxlsxwriter 210.9 ms mean versus Python XlsxWriter 919.1 ms (4.36x), with Python start-up and import inside the Python figure and no compiler, flags, libxlsxwriter build options, Python version or CPU stated; the same run puts rust_xlsxwriter with zlib ahead of C at 152.6 ms. Independent but via a wrapper: rOpenSci's writexl README times writexl (libxlsxwriter inside) at 12.3 s versus openxlsx2 at 19.6 s for nycflights13::flights (336,776 x 19), median of 2 runs, with equal file sizes.
status_note: Active (release 1.2.4 on 2026-01-06, security and memory fixes committed 2026-07-07), 1.8k stars, FreeBSD-variant BSD-2-Clause licence, copyable; the cited speedup is first-party with an undocumented build (the Makefile defaults to -O3, but CMake has no default build type), and the C row's 34.1 ms of system time versus 16.4 ms for Rust (derived from page data) is consistent with libxlsxwriter's default temp-file staging of each XML part, so a USE_MEM_FILE build may be faster than the published figure.
